records.sourceFile: The Influence of Sport-Field Properties on Muscle-Recruitment Patterns and Metabolic Response.pdf

paper.citation: Hales ME, Johnson JD II. The Influence of Sport-Field Properties on Muscle-Recruitment Patterns and Metabolic Response. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Eleven male athletes completed four agility circuits on two outdoor fields with different mechanical properties. Surface EMG, gas exchange, and 30-m sprint times were recorded before and after the circuits. The authors report that muscle activity differed between fields and that the field with greater energy return gave faster agility and sprint times, with largely similar metabolic responses.
paper.tldr: The surface a player trains on changed how 11 male athletes recruited their leg muscles during agility work. The lower energy-return field produced more muscle activity and slower agility times, so surface mechanics are worth considering in conditioning.
paper.methods: Eleven male athletes completed four consecutive agility circuits with 60 s rests on two outdoor fields, tested 7 days apart at the same time of day. Surface EMG was recorded from the vastus medialis, biceps femoris, gastrocnemius medial head and tibialis anterior, with a portable gas analyser for VO2, HR and energy expenditure. Field properties were measured with the ASTM F-1936 protocol, and 30-m sprints were run before and after the circuits.
paper.findings: Energy restitution was lower on Field A (28.2%) than Field B (41.6%), and force reduction and vertical deformation also differed. Summed muscle activity differed between fields (F(1,20) = 5.78, P = .026) and was higher on Field A in every trial (Table 2, for example T1 740.8 vs 566.6), and agility circuits took longer there (P = .02). Pretest 30-m sprints were slower on Field A (4.67 vs 4.31 s), and metabolic variables changed across trials but did not differ significantly between fields overall.
paper.limitations: Only 11 men and two fields were tested, with no injury outcomes, and the fatigue correlations were weak to moderate (r = .28 to .42). The EMG difference is reported as '<13%' in the abstract and 13% greater in the discussion, but the Table 2 means are about 30% higher on Field A. The field effect was analysed with field as a between-subject factor (F(1,20)) even though the same athletes ran on both fields.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend that player development staff consider a field's energy return and shock absorption when planning conditioning and training volume. They suggest preparing athletes on a surface with mechanical properties similar to the competition surface.
paper.athleteDev: Where possible, prepare athletes on surfaces that resemble the competition surface, and plan drills and volume knowing that energy return changes muscle activity and agility times. The study does not show that any specific footwear or training change improves performance.
paper.rtp: This study tested healthy athletes only and does not inform return-to-sport decisions or the timing of return after injury.

records.sourceFile: The Molecular Athlete - Exercise physiology from mechanisms to medals 2023.pdf

paper.citation: Furrer R, Hawley JA, Handschin C. The Molecular Athlete: Exercise Physiology from Mechanisms to Medals. Physiol Rev 2023;103:1693-1787.
paper.abstract: A review of skeletal muscle morphological, functional and molecular adaptations to endurance- and resistance-based training. It places these adaptations in the context of innate genetic and interindividual differences in exercise capacity, with particular attention to ageing athletes, and asks how adaptations translate from molecules to medals.
paper.tldr: Adaptation to elite training involves a broad set of molecular and tissue changes, and the upper limits of adaptation remain poorly understood. Training methods still rely heavily on trial and error, so the mechanistic research should be read as context rather than a ready prescription.
paper.methods: Narrative review covering skeletal muscle plasticity, oxygen transport, neuromuscular control, acute and chronic molecular mechanisms, muscle repair, genetics, ageing and the evolution of human movement, with a section on whether everyone can become an elite athlete. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: The authors summarise the morphological, functional and signalling changes behind endurance and resistance adaptation, noting that insight into endurance-training regulation far exceeds that for resistance training and that the mechanisms of detraining and muscle memory remain rudimentary. Individual responses form a continuum, apparent non-responders may respond when training volume or intensity is increased, and evidence linking specific genetic variants to elite performance is weak. Exercise-mimetic compounds show no evidence of performance enhancement in humans, may reduce training adaptation, and may carry serious risks.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, with no described search or grading of evidence, and many mechanistic findings come from rodent and cell models. The authors acknowledge major gaps in understanding how training signals are integrated, how cross-talk between muscle and other tissues works, and where adaptive limits lie.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors argue for closer links between basic science, sport science and coaches, and for personalised, evidence-based training. They suggest physical performance testing is likely more useful than commercial genetic testing for stratifying athletes, and caution against unvalidated compounds and quick fixes.
paper.athleteDev: Use the mechanistic picture as background for training design rather than as a fixed prescription, since endurance adaptation is better characterised than resistance adaptation and individual response varies. Avoid compounds marketed as exercise mimetics, because human performance evidence for them is absent.
paper.rtp: The review covers training adaptation in healthy and elite athletes and does not study injured athletes or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Rehabilitation is mentioned only in passing.

records.sourceFile: The Optimum Power Load_- A Simple and Powerful Tool for Testing and Training.pdf

paper.citation: Loturco I, Dello Iacono A, Nakamura FY, Freitas TT, Boullosa D, Valenzuela PL, et al. The Optimum Power Load: A Simple and Powerful Tool for Testing and Training. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022;17(2):151-159.
paper.abstract: The optimum power load (OPL) is the load that maximizes power output in an exercise. It is derived from the load-velocity relationship using only bar force and bar velocity, and is assessed with a simple incremental test based on percentages of body mass. This brief review summarizes the evidence on OPL-based testing and training, including its links with sport performance, its use in post-activation potentiation protocols, and its effects on strength, speed, power, body composition and endurance. The authors conclude that OPL-based schemes are valid and simple, and can be used by coaches and sport scientists across sports and populations.
paper.tldr: The optimum power load is a quick test that finds the load giving peak bar power, using set percentages of body mass. This review argues it is a simple, practical tool for testing athletes, setting training loads and choosing warm-up loads before power work.
paper.methods: Brief narrative review of published OPL studies. No systematic search or quality appraisal method is described.
paper.findings: Bar power at the OPL correlated moderately to very largely with sprint and vertical jump performance in several sports (for example r = .43 to .86 in young soccer players). It discriminated between sports, performance levels and sexes. OPL-based training produced similar or slightly greater strength, speed and power changes than traditional strength-power methods, with less total weight lifted and less neuromuscular fatigue. The authors also report that OPL-based potentiation protocols likely produce larger potentiation than heavy-load (above 85% 1RM) protocols, based on a limited number of studies.
paper.limitations: The review does not explain how studies were chosen or how their quality was judged. Most of the evidence is short term, and the authors acknowledge a lack of long-term OPL trials. The endurance findings come from a few cyclist studies without a control group that kept endurance training alone, and the body-composition evidence is scarce and mainly from cyclists, with one 6-week study finding no change. Correlations are not evidence of causation, as the authors note.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can find each athlete's OPL with an incremental bar-velocity test at set percentages of body mass and re-check it regularly, for example weekly. The authors suggest loads 20% above the OPL may suit change-of-direction and jump work and loads 20% below may suit short-sprint work, but this rests on a single cited study and is worded as 'possibly' more effective.
paper.athleteDev: The OPL test can be used to profile an athlete's bar power and set training loads. Training at the OPL produced similar or slightly greater strength, speed and power gains than traditional methods in the cited studies, with less total load and fatigue.
paper.rtp: The review does not cover injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot be used to judge readiness after injury. Its load recommendations apply to healthy athletes in training.

records.sourceFile: The Role of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) in Neuromuscular Adaptations - Implications for Strength and Power Development—A Review.pdf

paper.citation: Hung CH, Su CH, Wang D. The Role of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) in Neuromuscular Adaptations: Implications for Strength and Power Development - A Review. Life. 2025;15:657.
paper.abstract: The review examines peer-reviewed studies from 2000 to 2025 on how HIIT affects motor unit recruitment, fiber composition, neuromuscular efficiency, maximal strength, rate of force development, hypertrophy and power. It concludes that HIIT improves neural activation and explosive power, is less effective than resistance training for absolute strength and hypertrophy, and works best combined with resistance or plyometric training.
paper.tldr: Sprint-based and plyometric HIIT improve explosive power and rate of force development, but HIIT is not a replacement for heavy resistance training for maximal strength. The authors favour combining the two with periodization.
paper.methods: Narrative synthesis of literature found through PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and EBSCO using HIIT and neuromuscular keywords, covering 2000 to 2025, organized by theme. The text refers to 86 studies from its search, with no formal inclusion framework or meta-analysis.
paper.findings: The authors report that HIIT increases motor unit recruitment and synchronization, with greater fast-twitch activation, shifts toward Type II and hybrid IIa fibers, and improved rate of force development and explosive power. They report HIIT is less effective than traditional resistance training for maximal strength and hypertrophy because it lacks progressive heavy overload.
paper.limitations: No inclusion criteria, study counts by outcome, or quality grading are reported. The authors note long-term effects are understudied and data for youth and rehabilitation populations are sparse. Mechanistic claims are narrative and not graded for strength of evidence.
paper.practicalImplications: Use sprint-based or plyometric HIIT to support explosive power and rate of force development, and keep heavy resistance training in the program for maximal strength and muscle size. Schedule HIIT so it does not reduce force output in lifting sessions, and individualize intensity and work-to-rest ratios.
paper.athleteDev: Use HIIT, especially sprint and plyometric formats, as a time-efficient complement to strength training for explosive power, not as a replacement for heavy lifting. Sequence and periodize it to limit fatigue interference with strength work.
paper.rtp: Return to play is mentioned only briefly, as early-phase neuromuscular rehabilitation, and injured athletes were not studied. The review cannot be used to set return-to-sport timelines or clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: The Translation of Sport Science Research to the Field- A Current Opinion and Overview on the Perceptions of Practitioners, Researchers and Coaches.pdf

paper.citation: Fullagar HHK, McCall A, Impellizzeri FM, Favero T, Coutts AJ. The Translation of Sport Science Research to the Field: A Current Opinion and Overview on the Perceptions of Practitioners, Researchers and Coaches. Sports Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: A current opinion that reviews published survey and interview evidence on how practitioners, researchers and coaches acquire, value and apply sport science research. It also reviews the barriers that limit use of research in elite sport.
paper.tldr: Coaches mostly learn through personal conversation and value research on tactics, technique and mental training, while practitioners and researchers prioritise fitness and recovery. Aligned goals, embedded research staff and coach-focused research may help close the gap between research and practice.
paper.methods: Opinion piece reviewing published survey and interview studies of practitioners, researchers and coaches on how they source information, which research areas they value, and what barriers limit application. No search strategy is described, and the authors summarise the evidence in two tables and offer recommendations.
paper.findings: Coaches prefer personal contact and experience, such as conversations with players and other coaches, over courses or journals, and they rate their knowledge highest in tactical and technical areas. Coaches value research on mental training, tactics and technical efficiency most, while practitioners and researchers value fitness and recovery research and rate research embedded in clubs as most applicable. Reported barriers include funding and time for practitioners, staff and manager buy-in for researchers, and research questions that do not match coaches' needs.
paper.limitations: The paper describes itself as an opinion piece and reports no search method, so the evidence base cannot be audited. The cited data come from surveys of specific groups, such as 75 professional football coaches, 321 Turkish coaches and 205 Canadian coaches, and the authors note that peer-reviewed evidence on coaches' perceptions is limited. The recommendations were not tested.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners should tailor research to coaches' priorities, such as tactical or mental training questions, and present it through conversation, case studies or simple graphs rather than journal articles alone. Organisations could agree shared goals, define each role, and fund embedded or applied research that answers the questions coaches actually ask.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Introduce new monitoring or analysis only after agreeing a shared performance goal and each person's role with the coach. Present the findings in the format the coach prefers, since the paper reports that coaches favour conversation, case studies and simplified graphs.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The paper concerns how coaches and practitioners use sport science research in general, not return-to-play decisions. It cannot be used to judge which return-to-play tests or criteria are valid.

records.sourceFile: The acute demands of repeated sprint training on physiological, neuromuscular, perceptual and performance outcomes in team sport athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Thurlow F, Weakley J, Townshend AD, Timmins RG, Morrison M, McLaren SJ. The Acute Demands of Repeated-Sprint Training on Physiological, Neuromuscular, Perceptual and Performance Outcomes in Team Sport Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of 176 studies (908 samples) of overground repeated-sprint training in team sport athletes aged 16 or over. Pooled reference estimates were 163 bpm average heart rate, 10.7 mmol/L end-set blood lactate and 5.0% sprint decrement. Shuttle-based sprints, longer sprint distances and shorter inter-repetition rest increased or altered physiological and performance demands, while two fewer repetitions per set had a trivial effect on most outcomes.
paper.tldr: Repeated-sprint training is physically demanding for team sport athletes, with pooled blood lactate of about 10.7 mmol/L. Longer sprints and shorter rest raise the demand, while dropping from six to four repetitions per set changed most outcomes very little.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided systematic search of PubMed, SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE and Scopus (to January 2022) for original studies of overground running repeated-sprint training in team sport athletes aged 16 or over. Data were pooled with multilevel mixed-effects meta-analysis, and programming moderators (sprint modality, repetitions per set, sprint distance, rest modality and rest duration) were tested by meta-regression against a reference of 6 x 30 m straight sprints with 20 s passive rest. Effects were judged against practical thresholds as trivial, substantial or inconclusive.
paper.findings: Pooled estimates across protocols were average heart rate 163 bpm (90% CI 154 to 171), peak heart rate 182 bpm, end-set blood lactate 10.7 mmol/L, session RPE 6.5 deciMax, best sprint time 5.52 s and sprint decrement 5.0% (90% CI 4.7 to 5.3). Compared with the 6 x 30 m, 20 s passive rest reference, shuttle-based sprints increased average and best sprint times (1.42 s and 1.55 s slower) with a trivial effect on session RPE. Two more repetitions per set had trivial effects on most outcomes. A 10 m longer sprint increased blood lactate by 2.7 mmol/L and sprint decrement by 1.7%. A 10 s longer rest lowered blood lactate by 1.1 mmol/L and sprint decrement by 1.4%, with trivial effects on peak heart rate and session RPE. Active rest and rest modality effects were largely inconclusive.
paper.limitations: CMJ height, creatine kinase and peak heart rate as a percentage of maximum had too few comparable samples to be meta-analysed, and moderators could not be tested for average heart rate or VO2. Many moderator effects had confidence intervals spanning trivial and substantial effects, and part of the variation reflected factors not modelled, such as age, fitness, sex, number of sets and data collection methods. Some values were digitised from figures or estimated rest times, samples were removed when authors could not clarify protocols, and the review excluded injured athletes and sprints at 30 C or above.
paper.practicalImplications: To raise physiological demand and sprint decrement, longer sprint distances (over 30 m) and shorter rest (20 s or less) are the most consistent levers. To limit fatigue and protect sprint times, shorter sprints (15 to 25 m) with 30 s or more passive rest are suggested. Reducing from six to four repetitions per set changed most measured demands only trivially, so it may cut sprint volume without much loss of stimulus on average.
paper.athleteDev: Sprint distance and rest duration can be set to target either higher metabolic and fatigue stress (longer sprints, shorter rest) or better sprint quality (shorter sprints, longer rest). Four rather than six repetitions per set kept most demands similar on average, so it may be used to lower sprint volume, though the effect for an individual athlete may differ.
paper.rtp: The review included only healthy, non-injured athletes and excluded injured or returning athletes, so its demand estimates cannot set return-to-sport loading. The authors suggest gradually increasing sprint distance as a late-stage return-to-play progression, but this was not studied in injured athletes and should be treated as an untested extrapolation.

records.sourceFile: The effect of fatiguing muscle contractions on kicking performance in experienced soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Carstensen JB, Gaemelke T, Overgaard K, Andersen TB. The effect of fatiguing muscle contractions on kicking performance in experienced soccer players. Sports Biomechanics. 2024.
paper.abstract: Sixteen male soccer players (5 professional, 11 amateur) completed kicking tests after a fatiguing quadriceps protocol or rest, on separate days in a randomised crossover design. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction force, stimulation force ratio and kicking speed and accuracy were measured before and after each condition.
paper.tldr: Fatiguing the quadriceps lowered maximal kicking ball speed in experienced soccer players. Shooting accuracy did not change significantly, although the study was too small to rule out an effect.
paper.methods: Randomised crossover with 16 analysed male players (17 recruited, one dropout) from amateur to professional level, aged 18 to 30 years with at least 10 years of organised play. On separate days, participants completed a fatiguing protocol (5 sets of 10 maximal voluntary concentric and eccentric knee extensions with the kicking leg) or a rest control. Maximal isometric force, the 15 Hz/50 Hz stimulation force ratio, maximum ball speed, foot speed and shooting accuracy were measured before and after. Paired t-tests and repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni correction were used.
paper.findings: The fatiguing protocol reduced maximal isometric force by 14.0 +/- 2.7% and the force ratio by 14.0 +/- 3.7%, with no reduction in control. Maximum ball speed fell 1.9% after fatigue (0.57 m/s), with no change on the control day, and the change differed significantly between conditions (2.1%). Maximum foot speed fell 5.87% after fatigue, but the between-day difference was not significant (p = 0.054). Shooting accuracy improved 13.3% on the control day (p = 0.02) but did not change on the fatigue day, and the between-condition difference was not significant (p = 0.18). The short axis of the kick dispersion ellipse widened by 53.9% after fatigue, significantly more than on the control day.
paper.limitations: Only 16 players were analysed, and the authors state there was insufficient power for the accuracy outcome. The control-day accuracy improvement was unexpected by the authors and shows why a control condition matters when judging fatigue effects. Ball and foot speed were taken from each player's hardest kick, and accuracy kicks below 80% of maximum speed were discarded without being counted. Fatigue was induced in one muscle group with knee extensions, not match conditions. The ball-speed effect was small, at about 2%.
paper.practicalImplications: Heavy quadriceps work can reduce maximum kicking speed in trained players for at least the 30 minutes or so of testing that followed. The study found no clear effect on accuracy, so it does not show that fatigue harms shot placement. Practitioners should not assume a shooting-accuracy loss from this evidence.
paper.athleteDev: Fatiguing quadriceps work lowered maximum kick speed by about 2% in this group, but accuracy was not clearly affected. The study did not test how to sequence strength work and shooting practice.
paper.rtp: This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy players with an induced quadriceps fatigue protocol and included no injury or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: The effect of heat acclimation on critical environmental limits and rate of rectal temperature change.pdf

paper.citation: van den Bogaard T, Klous L, Cottle RM, Van Erp J, Daanen HAM. The effect of heat acclimation on critical environmental limits and rate of rectal temperature change. J Appl Physiol. 2025;138:1150-1160.
paper.abstract: The study quantified how heat acclimation changes the critical environmental limit (WBGTcrit, the point where heat balance can no longer be maintained) and the rate of rectal temperature rise during exercise in the heat. Twenty-eight unacclimatized adults were split into a heat acclimation group, which completed 5 to 9 days of controlled-hyperthermia cycling in 35 C and 65% humidity, and a control group. WBGTcrit increased after 9 but not 5 days, and rectal temperature rise was only reduced 4 to 8 days after the protocol ended.
paper.tldr: In active adults, 9 days of controlled-hyperthermia heat acclimation raised the heat level they could tolerate before core temperature kept climbing, but 5 days did not. The gain was still present 4 to 8 days after heat exposure stopped.
paper.methods: Participants (heat acclimation 6 men and 9 women; control 6 men and 7 women; VO2max about 46 mL/kg/min) were matched on body mass, VO2max, sex, age and body surface area and allocated by available time. The acclimation group completed progressive heat stress tests (cycling at fixed heat production in 38 C with stepwise rising humidity) before, after 5 and 9 days of acclimation, and after 4 or 8 days without heat; controls completed two tests about 13 days apart. WBGTcrit was set by visual inspection of the rectal temperature curve, and analyses used mixed-model and repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: WBGTcrit showed a group by time interaction (P = 0.016), rising from 28.5 to 30.5 C WBGT after 9 days in the acclimation group with no change after 5 days. The rate of rectal temperature rise showed no group by time interaction (P = 0.537); within the acclimation group it was lower 4 to 8 days after cessation than at baseline (0.6 versus 0.9 C/h). After 9 days, sweat loss rose by 165 mL/h and starting rectal temperature fell by 0.44 C relative to controls, and only starting rectal temperature showed decay after cessation.
paper.limitations: Visual identification of WBGTcrit left many missing values, so only 6 to 7 acclimation participants contributed to the key analyses, and an objective segmented-regression method did not reproduce the visual result (r = 0.33). Groups were not randomized, rectal temperature responds slowly, and 9 days may not be the minimum effective dose. Controls also showed unexplained drops in skin temperature and heart rate between tests.
paper.practicalImplications: With a controlled-hyperthermia protocol in warm-humid conditions, 5 days of heat acclimation did not raise the critical heat limit, while 9 days did. A short gap of 4 to 8 days without heat exposure after acclimation did not erase the WBGTcrit gain in this sample.
paper.athleteDev: For athletes preparing for hot competition or preseason, the data suggest planning more than 5 days of controlled-hyperthermia heat sessions if the goal is a higher heat tolerance limit. The sample was active adults rather than athletes, so magnitudes may differ in trained athletes.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions after injury or heat illness. It measured heat tolerance in healthy adults and did not study recovery from exertional heat illness.

records.sourceFile: The effectiveness of a practical half time re warm up strategy on performance and the physical response to soccer specific activity.pdf

paper.citation: Fashioni E, Langley B, Page RM. The effectiveness of a practical half-time re-warm-up strategy on performance and the physical response to soccer-specific activity. J Sports Sci. 2020;38(2):140-149.
paper.abstract: The authors compared a half-time re-warm-up with a passive half-time break in 10 male soccer players completing a 60-minute soccer-specific protocol. The re-warm-up improved 20 m sprint time, squat jump and countermovement jump after the re-warm-up and early in the second half, with no significant change in 5 m or 10 m sprint, muscle soreness or PlayerLoad. Ratings of perceived exertion were higher after the re-warm-up.
paper.tldr: A 3-minute bodyweight and plyometric re-warm-up at the end of a 15-minute half-time raised jump height right after half-time and gave a faster 20 m sprint 10 minutes into the second half in amateur players. It also raised perceived exertion, and the effects were short-term.
paper.methods: Randomised, counterbalanced crossover trial with 10 male amateur soccer players. Each completed 4 x 15-minute periods of the SAFT90 soccer-specific protocol with a 15-minute half-time, either passive (control) or passive 12 minutes plus a 3-minute re-warm-up of jogging, skipping, dynamic stretches, tuck jumps and sprints. Sprint, squat jump, countermovement jump, heart rate, perceived exertion, muscle soreness and PlayerLoad were compared with two-way repeated-measures models and minimal detectable differences.
paper.findings: Squat jump (30.17 vs 26.96 cm; d = 0.6) and countermovement jump height (31.53 vs 28.15 cm; d = 0.7) were higher immediately after half-time with the re-warm-up, and 20 m sprint time was faster at 55 minutes (3.32 vs 3.42 s; d = 0.6). Heart rate was higher straight after the re-warm-up, and perceived exertion was 1 to 2 units higher at 50, 55 and 60 minutes. No significant trial by time interactions were found for 5 m or 10 m sprint, muscle soreness or PlayerLoad.
paper.limitations: Only 10 amateur male players were studied, in a simulated protocol rather than match play, and the authors note the response may be specific to their methods and participant level. The 20 m sprint and squat jump differences fell within the range of the minimal detectable difference, squat jump height was not maintained and was lower than control at 55 minutes (moderate effect, not significant), and mechanisms were not measured.
paper.practicalImplications: A short, equipment-free re-warm-up at the end of half time produced acute jump and 20 m sprint gains early in the second half without changing soreness or PlayerLoad. It also raised perceived exertion in the second half, which the authors suggest may reflect the unfamiliar routine.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the study supports a 3-minute bodyweight and plyometric re-warm-up as a feasible half-time option, with small acute gains in jump and 20 m sprint performance in the first minutes of the second half. The jump benefit faded within the first post-half-time testing block.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The participants were healthy amateur players and the outcomes were acute performance measures only.

records.sourceFile: The effects of lower limb wearable resistance on sprint running performance - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Feser EH, Macadam P, Cronin JB. The effects of lower limb wearable resistance on sprint running performance: a systematic review. European Journal of Sport Science. 2020;20(3):394-406.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of ten studies (116 participants) on lower-limb wearable resistance during sprint running. Micro-loads of 0.6 to 5% body mass increased contact time and reduced step frequency, sprinting with 5% body-mass loads slowed total sprint time, unloaded sprints straight after WR use showed no significant change in total sprint time, and one longitudinal study in untrained participants found no significant change in maximal sprinting speed.
paper.tldr: Lower-limb wearable resistance of up to 5% body mass mainly changes sprint mechanics, increasing contact time and reducing step frequency, with stride length largely unchanged. Its effect on sprint performance is small and has been little studied in training.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA guidance. PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science were searched from inception to November 2018 with Boolean terms for limb, sprint and resistance. Eligible studies measured acute kinematic, kinetic or performance effects, or longitudinal effects, of lower-limb wearable resistance in injury-free participants. Of 692 records, ten were included and effect sizes were calculated as Cohen's d.
paper.findings: Eight studies measured acute kinematics. Loads of 0.6 to 5% body mass on the thigh, shank or whole leg increased contact time (2.9 to 8.9%) and reduced step frequency (1.4 to 3.7%), while stride length was largely unchanged. While sprinting with the loads, only 5% body-mass WR significantly slowed total sprint time (by 2.0% and 3.3% in two studies), and in the three acute performance studies unloaded sprints after WR use showed no significant change in total sprint time. The one six-week study of 5% ankle loading in untrained participants increased stride length and reduced stride frequency without a significant change in maximal speed.
paper.limitations: The included studies were small and mostly single-session, and the training study had a single post-test, so the effects of off-loading are unknown. Force production was not measured directly in most studies, and no information on the start and acceleration phases was given for the training study. The abstract reports total sprint time slowing of 0.6 to 7.4%, while the results text says only 5% body-mass loads produced a significant change in total sprint time.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches can use lower-limb loads of up to about 5% body mass to target step frequency and contact time in short sprint work. Loads should be progressed gradually because added rotational inertia may raise injury risk, and the review does not show that this improves sprint times.
paper.athleteDev: Lower-limb wearable resistance can overload stride frequency and may encourage more horizontal force in acceleration work, with stride length unchanged. Its effect on sprint speed is not established.
paper.rtp: The review includes only injury-free participants and does not study rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play loading decisions.

records.sourceFile: The effects of mental fatigue on sport-specific motor performance among team sport athletes - A systematic scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Yuan R, Sun H, Soh KG, Mohammadi A, Toumi Z, Zhang Z. The effects of mental fatigue on sport-specific motor performance among team sport athletes: a systematic scoping review. Frontiers in Psychology. 2023;14:1143618.
paper.abstract: Scoping review of studies on how mental fatigue affects physical and technical sport-specific performance in team sport athletes. Mental fatigue impaired physical performance, measured as intermittent endurance and total distance, and technical performance in most studies, with small-sided game results more mixed.
paper.tldr: Mental fatigue from prolonged cognitive tasks tends to reduce endurance and technical skill in team sport athletes, especially in laboratory tests. Effects on small-sided game distance are less consistent.
paper.methods: Scoping review using the Arksey and O'Malley framework, with a search run between March and May 2022 (no date restrictions) of Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, EBSCOhost databases, Google Scholar and grey literature. Eligible studies were randomised controlled trials in healthy team-sport athletes that compared a mentally fatiguing task with control and measured sport-specific physical or technical performance. Of 431 records, 18 met criteria at full-text stage, and 16 were retained after QualSyst quality appraisal.
paper.findings: Eleven studies examined physical performance. Intermittent endurance fell after mental fatigue in several soccer, cricket and Australian football studies (for example, Yo-Yo IR1 distance of 1,203 m vs 1,410 m in one soccer study), while small-sided game distance was unchanged in some studies. Eleven studies examined technical performance, with impairments in ball losses, passing and shooting errors, and tackling in most soccer, basketball and Australian football studies. Perceived exertion rose in most studies that measured it.
paper.limitations: Only English-language studies were included, and the review covers physical and technical skill but not perceptual-cognitive performance. Study counts are internally inconsistent (12 in the abstract, 16 in the methods and results, 19 in the psychophysiological section), and the number of studies per sport and format is small.
paper.practicalImplications: Prolonged cognitively demanding work before training or matches may reduce endurance and skill execution, so coaches could plan the timing of cognitive workload around skill and conditioning sessions. The studies used induced fatigue in experiments, so the size of the effect in real competition is unknown.
paper.athleteDev: Mental fatigue from prolonged cognitive tasks reduced endurance and technical outputs in most team-sport studies, so the timing of cognitive workload before skill or conditioning sessions is worth considering.
paper.rtp: The review includes only healthy athletes without injury and does not address return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: The effects of repeated sprint training on physical fitness and physiological adaptation in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Thurlow F, Huynh M, Townshend A, McLaren SJ, James LP, Taylor JM, et al. The Effects of Repeated-Sprint Training on Physical Fitness and Physiological Adaptation in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2023.
paper.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies of running-based repeated-sprint training (RST) in trained athletes aged 14 to 35. RST produced moderate gains in VO2max, Yo-Yo intermittent recovery distance and repeated-sprint decrement, and small gains in sprint, repeated-sprint average time, jump and change-of-direction measures. Changes to programming compared with a reference program gave little clear benefit.
paper.tldr: Running repeated-sprint training improves aerobic fitness, intermittent running, sprint speed and jump height in trained athletes. Three sets of six 30 m sprints, twice weekly for 6 weeks, was effective and is a reasonable starting prescription.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Scopus searched to 4 July 2023, registered on the Open Science Framework. Included trained or higher-calibre athletes aged 14 to 35 in running RST of 10 s or less with 60 s or less rest for 2 to 12 weeks; quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black index, and multilevel meta-analysis and meta-regression were run against a reference program of three sets of 6 x 30 m, twice weekly for 6 weeks.
paper.findings: Pooled effects (Table 2, 90% CI) were VO2max 0.63 (0.36 to 0.91), YYIR1 0.60 (0.43 to 0.77), RSA decrement -0.63 (-0.86 to -0.40), 10 m sprint -0.34 (-0.47 to -0.21), 20 m sprint -0.45 (-0.69 to -0.21), CMJ height 0.27 (0.14 to 0.39) and change of direction -0.32 (-0.53 to -0.12). Compared with the reference program, one more session per week, one more week, 200 m more volume, two more reps, one more set or 10 m more distance was either non-substantial or came with compatibility with impairment in at least one outcome.
paper.limitations: The abstract's effect sizes differ from Table 2 (VO2max 0.56 vs 0.63, 20 m sprint -0.48 vs -0.45, RSA decrement -0.61 vs -0.63, YYIR1 0.61 vs 0.60, CMJ 0.26 vs 0.27). Table 3 lists VO2max as 2.6 ml/kg/min while the text gives 2.2, and the YYIR1 raw-unit CI reads '1534 to 296', which is a typo. About a third of studies (13 of 40) had no control group, all RST was done alongside usual training, and the review could not model sprint modality or rest duration.
paper.practicalImplications: Three sets of six 30 m straight-line sprints with 20 s passive rest, twice weekly for 6 weeks, is an effective default block. Four sets per session added to intermittent running gains, and a third weekly session impaired change-of-direction ability, so the authors advise against three weekly sessions outside short 2-week blocks.
paper.athleteDev: Use 3 sets of 6 x 30 m, twice weekly for 6 weeks, as a time-efficient block, with 4 to 6 reps per set. A third weekly session did not add benefit and impaired change of direction in the reference comparison, so reserve it for short shock blocks.
paper.rtp: Limited return-to-sport use: the authors mention late-stage return-to-play as a possible use, but all included athletes were healthy and uninjured, so the data cannot set return-to-play sprint loads.

records.sourceFile: The effects of velocity loss thresholds during resistance training on lower-limb performance enhancement - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Chen BY, Chen WH, Liu Y, Fiolo NJ, Fuchs PX, Huang CF, et al. The effects of velocity loss thresholds during resistance training on lower-limb performance enhancement: A systematic review with meta-analysis. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024:1-15.
paper.abstract: Meta-analysis of 13 studies (308 participants) of back-squat training with low (0 to 20%) or high (30 to 45%) velocity loss thresholds. Low thresholds gave larger heavy-load squat velocity, light-load squat velocity and sprint gains, while maximal strength gains were similar between thresholds.
paper.tldr: Squat sets stopped at about 20% velocity loss gave better speed and power gains than sets allowed to lose 30 to 45%, while maximal strength changed similarly. Coaches may prefer low thresholds when speed or power is the goal.
paper.methods: PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021247929) of five databases searched in May 2023. Included peer-reviewed randomised trials of back-squat training of at least 4 weeks that used velocity monitoring and ended sets at a set velocity loss threshold; effects were pooled as Hedges g with random-effects models, and meta-regression was run on linear-progression studies only.
paper.findings: Between-group differences favoured low thresholds for heavy-load squat velocity (ES -0.40, p = 0.005), light-load squat velocity (ES -0.39, p = 0.025) and sprint time (ES -0.47, p = 0.022). The CMJ difference (ES -0.24, p = 0.088) and 1RM difference (ES -0.65, p = 0.630) were not significant, and 0-10% vs 20% thresholds did not differ significantly on any outcome.
paper.limitations: The abstract and discussion describe the CMJ advantage of low thresholds as superior although p = 0.088, which is not significant. The sprint meta-regression p value is 0.010 in the abstract and discussion but 0.002 in the results. High-threshold group labels also vary between 30 to 40% and 30 to 45% across the text and figures, and the studies were short, squat-only programs.
paper.practicalImplications: For speed or jump goals, stopping squat sets at about 20% velocity loss or less is the best-supported option. The authors' 10% or less recommendation for sprint rests on the meta-regression, since direct 0-10% vs 20% comparisons showed no significant difference; for maximal strength alone, a 0 to 40% range gave similar gains.
paper.athleteDev: Use a velocity loss of 20% or less on squat sets when the goal is speed, power or jump height; the authors suggest 10% or less when sprint time is the priority, but this is less certain. Strength-only blocks can tolerate wider thresholds, but the review did not test these over a full training season.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return to sport: all included trials used healthy, non-injured, resistance-trained people, and no rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes were assessed.

records.sourceFile: The impact of different warm‐up strategies on acceleration and deceleration demands in highly trained soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Silva H, Nakamura FY, Bajanca C, Pinho G, Loturco I, Marcelino R. The impact of different warm-up strategies on acceleration and deceleration demands in highly trained soccer players. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024;24:88-96.
paper.abstract: Nineteen highly trained U23 soccer players were tracked with 10 Hz GPS over four weeks across Reaction Speed, Run and Speed warm-up strategies. Speed warm-ups produced the highest acceleration and deceleration demands, and all strategies produced fewer than one high-intensity effort per minute.
paper.tldr: Warm-up type changes how much acceleration and deceleration a soccer player performs, so warm-ups should be monitored as their own load rather than folded into the session total. Speed-based warm-ups were the most demanding and should be planned with the next match or session in mind.
paper.methods: A cross-sectional GPS study (10 Hz) of 19 outfield players across 19 training sessions, in which coaches assigned Reaction Speed (8 to 15 min), Run (9 to 14 min) or Speed (14 to 20 min) warm-ups. Acceleration and deceleration efforts were classified by relative intensity against each player's mesocycle maximum and by starting speed, and compared with paired effect sizes.
paper.findings: Speed warm-ups produced more high-intensity accelerations than Reaction Speed (ES 0.74, 90% CI 0.21 to 1.33) and more efforts starting above 20 km/h, and Reaction Speed produced more moderate-intensity accelerations than Run (ES 1.29). Run was the least demanding, with no high-intensity accelerations and no efforts above 25 km/h. Position differences emerged only within the Run warm-up.
paper.limitations: One team, one coaching staff and four weeks of sessions limit generalization, and warm-up assignment was not randomized. The intensity bands depend on each player's maximum within the mesocycle, and the warm-ups were not standardized protocols such as FIFA 11+, which limits replication.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest matching the warm-up to the work that follows: Reaction Speed before technical-tactical sessions, Speed before high-intensity sessions and Run before longer or moderate sessions, and avoiding Speed warm-ups close to competition. These are untested recommendations, but monitoring the starting speed of repeated efforts follows from its strong effect on acceleration and deceleration counts.
paper.athleteDev: Log warm-up type and count acceleration and deceleration efforts by starting speed, so warm-up load is tracked alongside the rest of the session.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return to sport, because it measured healthy training players and included no injured or rehabilitating athletes.
